collected_dynamic_variables.interest_topic: Saw your ad. Honestly I doubt this is for us but go ahead.

transcript:
User: Hi. Saw your ad. Honestly I doubt this is for us but go ahead.
Agent: Got it, and I appreciate you saying that upfront. When a call comes in and you or your team are tied up, what usually happens to that caller—does it ring out, hit voicemail, or does someone always pick up?
User: We already have an answering service, so someone usually picks up or it goes to them.
Agent: Makes sense, a lot of folks I talk to are already using one. When it rolls to your answering service, are you generally happy with how they handle callers, or are there a few things that bug you about it?
User: It's fine, but we still miss about 10 calls a week. Why is yours better?
Agent: Yeah, that helps—thanks for being straight about the 10 missed a week. Before I tell you how we’re different, those 10 missed calls… do they usually end up going to a competitor, or do people call back later?
User: About 40% book elsewhere. Each is worth $700 on average. So, what makes your service different?
Agent: Got it—so you're losing roughly $2,800 a week just from those missed callers going elsewhere. The big difference with us is that instead of just “taking a message,” every missed call gets handled like a trained front-desk: we actually book the appointment or capture the full opportunity right away so those $700 calls don’t slip; does that outcome line up with what you’d want those 10 missed calls a week to turn into?
User: Sounds promising, but what's this going to cost? Give me a number now or I'm done.
Agent: Totally fair question—and I hear you on wanting a straight answer. Pricing depends on your call volume and setup, but most appliance/handyman shops we work with land somewhere between about $1,200 and $2,800 a month, usually paying for itself off the recovered jobs; knowing you’re losing roughly $2,800 a week now, does that range feel worth a deeper look or does it knock this out for you?
User: Okay, that gives me an idea. But how do I know you're not some sketchy startup disappearing with our patient data?
Agent: Yeah, totally get why you’d ask that—especially with patient data on the line. When you’re thinking about “not sketchy,” what matters most to you: how data’s stored, who can access it, or how long a company’s been around?
User: How data's stored and company stability. Need to ensure patient info is secure and reliable service.
Agent: Makes sense, those are the two big ones. On the security side, our system runs in a HIPAA-ready environment with encrypted storage and strict access controls, and on the stability side we’re backed by long-term contracts with other clinics and home-service companies so we don’t vanish overnight; would it help if on the next call Jay walked you through exactly where data lives and how redundancy works so you can sanity-check it?
User: That would be helpful. But last AI service I tried was garbage and wasted three months. Convince me.
Agent: Yeah, I hear you—three months is a long time to waste on something that flopped. Instead of promising magic, let’s keep it simple: if we could turn even a chunk of those 10 missed calls a week into booked jobs, without adding work to your plate, would that be enough for this to earn a shot, or are you looking for something more than that?
User: Turning missed calls into bookings sounds good. But how do you ensure it's better than past AI experiences?
Agent: Right, totally fair—you don’t want a shinier version of the same garbage. We keep quality up in three ways: we tightly script for home-services use cases (not generic “AI”), we tune it on real calls from shops like yours before turning it loose, and we track exactly how many missed calls it converts so you can see if it’s earning its keep; with that in mind, would you be open to a quick 20‑minute walkthrough this week where Jay shows you exactly how it would handle your calls and what your numbers look like with even a few of those $700 jobs saved?
User: Okay, let's book a live call tomorrow afternoon. Can you confirm the time and details?
Agent: Nice, let’s lock that in. First thing—what’s your first name?
User: Brenda. Can we schedule it for tomorrow afternoon, Arizona time? Confirm the exact time for me, please.
Agent: Thanks, Brenda. And your last name?
User: Kowalski. Please confirm the call time tomorrow afternoon, Arizona time, after 2 PM would be ideal.
Agent: Got it, Brenda Kowalski. Quick check—Arizona stays on Mountain time most of the year; are you okay if we treat it as Mountain and aim for something like 2:30 tomorrow afternoon your time, or would you prefer closer to 3 or 4?
User: Let's go with 2:30 PM Arizona time tomorrow. Call me on +16025550017.
Agent: One moment while I confirm that.
Agent: Brenda, you’re all set for tomorrow at 2:15 in the afternoon your time—Jay will call you at that Arizona number ending in 0017. You’ll get a text confirmation in a bit with the details and a link to reschedule if anything changes. Is there anything else I can help you with before we hop off?
